raw_response:
I'm 68 this year, and I've worked these 6 mu in Quzhou for half a century. When I was young, I studied at the agricultural college in Handan — soil chemistry, crop management, the whole system. That gave me a framework, but fifty years of droughts, price crashes, and watching my own back get stiffer taught me that the textbook target and the bank account reality are two different things. These days it's just me and my wife, so every decision balances what the crop could do against what two aging people can actually manage.

I run two systems on my 6 mu. Three and a half mu is stevia, my cash crop for the last 12 years. The buyer from the processing cooperative drives to my door. The remaining two and a half mu stays in wheat-maize double cropping — my grain security. I learned in 2009, when stevia prices collapsed to 6 yuan per jin, that monoculture is gambling. The wheat-maize system is my insurance.

**Stevia (3.5 mu)**

I'm transplanting improved seedlings in mid-to-late April. Certified stock from the county nursery costs about 550 yuan per mu — just under 2,000 yuan total. Two years ago I tried propagating my own cuttings to save money. The vigor was poor and I lost about 18% yield. When I ran the numbers, saving 550 yuan per mu cost me more in lost revenue than I saved. Never again.

For fertilizer, I'm targeting 16 kg N per mu. The extension sheet recommends 20, but I've tracked the yield response on this field over 12 years, and the last 4 kg of N barely pays for itself on my soil. I split it three ways: basal compound fertilizer (15-15-15, about 35 kg/mu) worked into the bed before transplanting, urea topdress at about 45 days when the plants start branching hard, and a lighter compound topdress before first harvest in mid-August. Total P and K from the compound comes to about 5 kg/mu each. The cooperative soil test two years back said my phosphorus and potassium were in the adequate range, so I don't chase higher rates — that's just burning cash.

Irrigation is metered well water at roughly 30 yuan per mu per round. I'll irrigate four times: right after transplanting for root establishment, mid-May during rapid vegetative growth, July at peak leaf expansion, and late August if the summer drought persists. I've compared three irrigations versus four over the years — three cuts yield by about 12%, which at current prices costs me more than the extra water. Five irrigations doesn't add meaningful yield.

Weeds are the main pest issue. I spray glyphosate pre-plant, then hand-weed twice. Stevia's bitter leaves mean insects mostly leave it alone. I haven't sprayed insecticide on stevia in five years, and I don't budget for it.

Tillage: rotary tillage in early April, then raised beds for transplanting. My wife's nephew brings his tractor — I pay him in dried leaves, no cash.

Labor: about 30 family days for 3.5 mu, from transplanting through drying and bagging. No hired labor — at 150 yuan per day, it would erase my margin.

Yield target: 500 kg/mu dried leaves. Last year: 480. Year before: 520. I'm expecting 500 in a normal year.

**Winter wheat (2.5 mu)**

The wheat went in last October. It's late March now, and the stand looks healthy — good tiller count, no winterkill. I'll topdress urea at jointing stage, around April 5th. I apply about 12 kg N per mu. The basal compound fertilizer I put down at planting last fall supplied roughly 5 kg P and 4 kg K per mu. No more phosphorus or potassium in spring — the soil test showed adequate levels, and adding more is waste.

I'll irrigate twice more this spring: once right after topdressing to wash the nitrogen down to the roots, and once at grain filling in mid-to-late May if we don't get rain. Wheat pays for its water — it's my food security.

One herbicide spray in early spring for wild oats, before the wheat gets too tall to walk through. That's it for pesticides.

Spring labor is light — about 4 family days for topdressing, irrigation, and scouting.

Yield target: 400 kg/mu. My ten-year average on this plot is 405.

**Summer maize (2.5 mu, same land)**

After wheat harvest in early June, I have maybe five days to turn the field around. That's the North China Plain double-crop reality — you don't hesitate. Hybrid seed at about 40 yuan per mu. All fertilizer goes down in one shot at planting: compound fertilizer in the seed furrow supplying 14 kg N, 4 kg P, and 3 kg K per mu. No side-dressing. The season is too short, and at 68 I'm not working fertilizer into standing corn in July heat.

Irrigation: one at planting if the soil is dry after wheat harvest, and one in mid-July. If the summer rains are decent, I might skip the July irrigation. Maize handles dry spells better than people think.

Herbicide at planting. I'll scout for corn borer in August — if the tunneling is heavy enough to matter, I'll spray. Otherwise, no preventive insecticide. I haven't done preventive spraying in three years.

Tillage: minimal. One quick rotary pass after wheat harvest, then plant immediately. If the stubble isn't too heavy, I direct-seed.

Labor: about 5 family days. Yield target: 450 kg/mu. I've been getting 430–470 consistently.

**Budget**

Total cash inputs this year: about 4,200 yuan. Stevia seedlings are the single biggest expense at just under 2,000 yuan. I keep 1,000 yuan in reserve. My wife takes blood pressure medication, and I will not zero our cash for a theoretical yield increment. That's the difference between managing a farm and optimizing a spreadsheet.
